title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One II
statement: The array `nums` holds only 0s and 1s. One operation picks an index `i` and inverts every element from `nums[i]` through the last element of the array (each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0). You may perform any number of operations, including none. Return the fewest operations after which every element of `nums` is 1.
notes:
## Intuition

Only an operation at index 0 can change `nums[0]`, and doing it twice changes nothing, so it is needed exactly when `nums[0]` is 0. Once that is settled, the same reasoning applies to index 1 with its current value, then index 2, and so on: scanning left to right, every element that is still 0 when reached forces an operation that starts there. Really inverting the suffix each time would cost O(n²), but the scan only needs to know whether the current element has been inverted an odd number of times.

## Approach

1. `operations` counts the operations made so far; `flipped` is true when an odd number of them cover the current position (every operation so far covers all later elements).
2. For each `num`, its current `value` is `num`, or `1 - num` when `flipped` is true.
3. If `value` is 0, start an operation here: increase `operations` and toggle `flipped` for everything from here on.
4. Return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]`.

- Index 0: value 0, so `operations = 1` and `flipped = true`.
- Index 1: the 1 now reads as 0, so `operations = 2` and `flipped = false`.
- Index 2: value 1, nothing to do.
- Index 3: value 0, so `operations = 3` and `flipped = true`.
- Index 4: the 1 reads as 0, so `operations = 4`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per element.
- Space: O(1): a counter and a flag.

## Pitfalls

- Testing the original `num` instead of its current value is wrong: `[0, 1]` needs 2 operations, not 1, because the first operation turns the 1 into 0.
- Toggle `flipped` rather than setting it to true; two operations covering an element cancel out.
- Physically inverting the suffix on every operation gives the right answer but is O(n²) for 10^5 elements.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `operations` | number of operations made so far |
| `flipped` | whether the current element is inverted by an odd number of operations |
| `num` | the element's original value |
| `value` | the element's value after the earlier operations |

narration.2: No operation has been made yet.
narration.3: flipped tells whether the elements from here on are currently inverted by an odd number of operations.
narration.5: Visit the elements left to right; later operations can never reach the ones already passed.
narration.6: Every earlier operation also inverted this element, so read its current value through flipped.
narration.7: A 0 here can only be fixed by an operation that starts at this index.
narration.9: It inverts this element and everything after it, so the parity changes.
narration.12: Every element is now 1; return the number of operations used.
